say.text: A 40-year-old is pulled from a house fire. Flame burns cover his face and neck. His voice is hoarse, and there is soot around his mouth.
You have just taken over his care. What do you do first?

choices.label: Work out the Parkland volume from the burn size
Secure the airway now and give 100% oxygen
Watch the airway; intubate only if it fails
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which part of the primary survey these burns put at risk, and what the burn sum can safely wait for.
You picked the fluid sum. A burn this size feels like a fluid problem, so the Parkland sum comes to mind first.
It misses the airway. Early intubation is decided before oedema develops, so the airway takes priority over the numbers.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this one properly: the sum is never the first move. Check the airway, then size the burn.

say.text: You picked watch and wait. He is talking and his airway sounds fine right now, so waiting looks safe.
Waiting for stridor or failing oxygen waits for the late signs. Hoarseness, soot and facial burns already call for a tube, while the airway is still easy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: waiting for the airway to fail is the trap. Act on the warning signs.

say.text: The airway can close as the swelling builds, while the fluid sum can wait until the airway is safe.
So the order is airway, then the burn size, then the fluid. The first two can be done in minutes; the airway cannot wait.
Yes. Airway first, because it is the part that can close while you work on the numbers. Intubate while the tube is still easy to pass.
The primary survey (ABCDE) comes first. Burns to the face, neck or mouth put the airway at risk, so high-flow 100% oxygen starts at once.
Intubate early, before oedema develops: hoarseness, stridor, deep facial or neck burns, soot in the mouth, or a falling level of consciousness.
He is talking comfortably now. The burn looks deep but the face is not yet swollen.
Why intubate early anyway?

choices.label: Swelling builds over hours, so a tube is easier now
Swelling matters when stridor or desaturation appears
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the airway will look like in a few hours, not how he sounds today.
You picked the sign-based model. He looks safe now, so you wait for the airway to show it is failing.
Stridor is a late sign. Hoarseness and soot already call for a tube, and oedema may be too far along to pass one once stridor shows.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the airway is judged by where the swelling is going, not by how he sounds today.

say.text: Early intubation is done before oedema develops, so a tube placed then is far easier than one placed after the swelling sets in.
Yes. The swelling is still building when he looks calm, so the tube goes in while the airway is easy.
Once the airway and breathing are safe, which task belongs to the secondary survey?

choices.label: Estimating the TBSA and depth of the burn
Working out the first eight hours of fluid
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of these is part of the first look at life threats, and which one only starts after that look is done.
You picked the fluid volume. It is the burn's own job, so it feels like the first thing a burn team should do.
Burn assessment, including TBSA and depth, belongs to the secondary survey, after ABCDE. The fluid sum is worked out after that.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this now: the fluid sum comes after the primary survey, not before it.

say.text: Yes. TBSA and depth are secondary-survey tasks, done once the airway and breathing are secured.
The order for a burn: airway first, with early intubation while the tube is still easy. Then breathing, circulation and the secondary survey.
Burn size and depth come next. The fluid sum is the last step of the plan, not the first.
